practicalQuestion: What should pre-training fueling and hydration prioritize for a collegiate athlete completing an early-morning high-intensity session when appetite is low and less than 45 minutes are available before training?

decisionContext.population: Collegiate athletes participating in high-intensity morning training
decisionContext.phase: Before an early-morning field or court session
decisionContext.outcome: Support session quality with a practical, tolerable intake approach
decisionContext.constraints: Low appetite; limited preparation time; individual gastrointestinal tolerance; no clinical nutrition condition

evidenceConfidence.rationale: No source tests what to eat or drink in the last 45 minutes before an early-morning session, or how to fuel when appetite is low. The closest guidance comes from a rugby league review table. Citing earlier guidelines for match days, it lists an optional 20 to 30 g carbohydrate snack or drink 30 to 60 minutes before kick-off, if hungry. Caffeine guidance places intake 30 to 60 minutes, or about 1 hour, before exercise. The rest of the evidence covers longer pre-exercise windows, match-day carbohydrate loading in two elite players, and hydration patterns in male football players during warm to hot outdoor preseason practices. These sources support planning, individual testing, and hydration monitoring. They do not settle the short-window question, so options are presented instead of a single direction.

dimensions.sourceReview: The sources are a narrative review of rugby league nutrition whose timing figures are drawn largely from earlier guidelines, a two-player case study, a narrative review of caffeine and sleep, a smart-bottle validation study that reported fluid balance as a secondary measure, an observational hydration study in high school American football, and a narrative review of heat preparation in elite athletes.
dimensions.directness: Indirect. The closest short-window guidance is a 20 to 30 g snack 30 to 60 minutes before a rugby league match, if hungry, and caffeine 30 to 60 minutes before a match. Both come from review tables or text citing earlier guidelines for matches. Neither was tested in training sessions. No source tests pre-exercise intake strategies for athletes with low appetite.
dimensions.consistency: The sources agree that strategies should be individualized and planned, and the caffeine timing figures are consistent with each other. No source tests competing short-window approaches, so consistency cannot be judged on the core question.
dimensions.transferability: The fueling and hydration data come from professional male rugby league players, elite male Australian football players, and high school and post-graduate male American football players. The heat and caffeine reviews summarize elite athletes of both sexes across sports. No primary data come from collegiate athletes, female team-sport athletes, or court sports.

bottomLine.text: No source tests intake in the last 45 minutes before an early-morning session, or strategies for low appetite. A rugby league review table, citing earlier guidelines for match days, lists 1 to 4 g/kg carbohydrate 1 to 4 hours before, lower-fiber choices closer to kick-off, and an optional 20 to 30 g light snack or drink 30 to 60 minutes before, only if hungry. Caffeine guidance places intake about 30 to 60 minutes before exercise. Hydration evidence supports planned, individualized fluid strategies and shows wide variation between athletes. Any short-window approach should be trialled in training and judged on individual tolerance.

actions.title: Option: move more fuel and fluid earlier
actions.text: The reported pre-exercise carbohydrate targets use a 1 to 4 hour window, and the same review lists 5 to 7 ml/kg of fluid 2 to 4 hours before a match. In one 2-player case study, a prescribed 24-hour high-carbohydrate diet plus a meal 4 hours before play was followed by prematch muscle glycogen above 500 mmol/kg dry weight, with no comparison condition. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): some staff may shift more carbohydrate and fluid to the previous evening and to any earlier waking window, so less needs to be taken in the final 45 minutes.

actions.title: Option: small, low-fiber intake in the window
actions.text: A rugby league review table, citing earlier guidelines for match days, lists an optional 20 to 30 g carbohydrate light snack or drink 30 to 60 minutes before kick-off, if hungry, and lower-fiber, higher glycemic index choices closer to kick-off. These figures were not tested in training sessions or in athletes with low appetite. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): if staff use a small, easy-to-tolerate carbohydrate source in the window, trial it in training first. This mirrors the heat-competition advice that strategies be pre-planned and practised.

actions.title: Plan hydration individually
actions.text: The smart-bottle study authors cite consensus that athletes follow personalized hydration practices, and a heat review describes pre-planned and practised hydration as best practice for competing in the heat. Fluid balance varied widely between athletes during early-morning practices in warm, humid conditions. In high school players practising in a hot environment, the authors report urine-color carryover between practices, mostly when practices were less than 24 hours apart. Body mass did not differ significantly from the end of one practice to the start of the next, and the authors advise replenishing fluids during and between practices. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): give closer attention to fluid intake after an evening session that precedes a morning session.

actions.title: Option: caffeine only if already individually tested
actions.text: The reported caffeine recommendation is about 3 to 6 mg/kg about 1 hour before exercise. In trials, caffeine was typically taken 60 minutes or less before testing, and the rugby league review suggests 30 to 60 minutes before a match. Responses vary between individuals. In the context of balancing performance against sleep effects, the caffeine review advises individual testing in simulated competitions that measure performance and unwanted effects. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): use caffeine only if it has already been tolerated in training, and confirm compliance with team, institutional, and governing-body rules first.

monitoring.label: Fluid balance
monitoring.text: In hot high school practices, urine color and urine specific gravity did not significantly identify body mass loss of 2% or more, but the players did not reach that level of loss. The authors note that multiple assessments, including urinary measures, reduce misclassification of hydration status. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): track pre-session to post-session body mass change alongside urine measures rather than relying on one measure.

monitoring.label: Tolerance and session quality
monitoring.text: Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): during practice trials, record gastrointestinal comfort and perceived session quality. This applies the cited advice to test caffeine individually in simulated conditions and to practise hydration strategies in advance.

guardrails.text: Treat the published carbohydrate, fluid, and caffeine figures as starting ranges drawn from match-day guidance in other populations. They are not tested targets for an early-morning training window. The 30 to 60 minute snack is listed only for athletes who are hungry. The review authors note there may not be enough data for sport-specific recommendations.
Do not use urine color or urine specific gravity alone to judge an athlete's hydration before training.

The rugby league review concludes that the sport nutritionist or dietitian should work with staff and players on individual nutrition plans. Professional judgment (not tested by the cited evidence): refer any athlete who develops a clinical nutrition concern, or who has persistent low appetite or gastrointestinal symptoms, to a registered dietitian or the medical team. This brief does not prescribe individual intake.

limitations.text: The fueling evidence comes from a narrative review of young professional male rugby league players, whose timing figures are largely drawn from earlier guidelines, and a case study of 2 elite male Australian football players. Both concern match play, not early-morning training.

The hydration evidence comes from male high school American football players in hot outdoor preseason practices, male post-graduate team players in warm, humid early-morning practices, and a review of elite athletes competing in heat. Transfer to cooler or indoor court sessions is uncertain.
The caffeine evidence comes from narrative reviews. They report timing of 30 to 60 minutes, or about 1 hour, before exercise and note that responses vary between individuals.

whatCouldChange.text: Studies testing small carbohydrate or fluid intakes taken less than 45 minutes before high-intensity morning team-sport training, including in athletes with low appetite, would allow a direct recommendation.
Evidence in collegiate, female, or court-sport athletes, or in cooler conditions, would show whether the hydration variation and carryover patterns transfer to this setting.

claims.text: A narrative review of young professional male rugby league players recommends that, for competition, players consume 1 to 4 g/kg carbohydrate plus 0.25 g/kg protein 1 to 4 hours before exercise, for 80 to 120 kg players. The authors note there may not be enough data to provide rugby-league-specific recommendations.

evidence.excerpt: Competition nutrition should maximize glycogen availability by consuming 1-4 g/kg carbohydrate (∼80-320 g) plus 0.25 g/kg (∼20-30 g) protein, 1-4 hr preexercise for 80-120 kg players.
Although there may not be enough data to provide RL-speciﬁc recommendations, the available data suggest that players may require approximately 6-8 g·kg−1·day−1 carbohydrate

claims.text: In a case study of 2 elite male Australian football forwards, a prescribed 24-hour diet of 8 g/kg carbohydrate plus a prematch meal of 2 g/kg carbohydrate eaten 4 hours before the match was followed by prematch muscle glycogen above 500 mmol/kg dry weight. Biopsies were taken only before and after the match, so there was no pre-loading comparison. The authors judged this level sufficient for elite match play.

evidence.excerpt: After a 24-h CHO-loading protocol of 8 and 2 g/kg in the prematch meal, 2 elite male forward players had biopsies sampled from m. vastus lateralis before and after participation in a South Australian Football League game.
4 hours prior to match play, each player also consumed a prematch
Conclusion: Prematch CHO loading elevated muscle glycogen concentrations (ie, >500 mmol/kg dw), the magnitude of which appears sufﬁcient to meet the metabolic demands of elite AF match play.

claims.text: A narrative review reports that the current caffeine recommendation is about 3 to 6 mg/kg taken about 1 hour before exercise.

evidence.excerpt: The current recommendation for caffeine supplementation is ingesting ~ 3-6 mg/kg about 1 h before the onset of exercise.

claims.text: The same review, which focuses on the conflict between using caffeine for performance and protecting sleep, reports that performance and sleep responses to caffeine vary between individuals and depend on session conditions such as time of onset. To resolve that conflict, it advises assessing athletes individually using simulated competitions that measure performance during exercise and unwanted effects in the following hours.

evidence.excerpt: Overall, the performance response to caffeine and the effect of this substance on sleep quality can vary interindividually and depend on the conditions of the exercise session (time of onset, duration, etc.).

nutritional practitioners should assess their athletes individually to resolve the conflict between caffeine ingestion and ensuring sleep quality on an individual basis, using simulated competitions with dual measurement of performance during exercise and unwanted effects in the following hours

claims.text: A narrative review of elite athletes preparing to compete in the heat describes best practice as heat acclimation complemented by pre-planned and practised cooling and hydration strategies used immediately before or during competition.

evidence.excerpt: Best practices to protect athlete health and performance during competition include heat acclimation/acclimatisation [(HA); i.e., long-term pre-competition preparation] complemented by pre-planned and practised cooling and hydration strategies (i.e., short-term interventions immediately before or during competition).

claims.text: In a smart-bottle validation study of 30 male post-graduate team American football athletes, testing took place during three early-morning outdoor preseason practices averaging 29.3 °C and 75% relative humidity, with players drinking ad libitum. Fluid balance, a secondary measure, ranged from a 2.35% loss to a 0.47% gain across athletes.

evidence.excerpt: Testing took place over the course of three pre-season outdoor practices held in the early mornings during 1 week in August.
Thirty male American football athletes drank from bottles equipped with a smart cap during outdoor pre-season practices (110 ± 30 min; 29.3 ± 3.0 °C; 75 ± 11% rh).
Fluid balance also varied substantially among athletes; ranging from 2.35% loss to 0.47% gain during the practice sessions
